parsed_answer.content: Type erasure is the mechanism by which the Java compiler enforces generic type constraints at compile-time while ensuring backward compatibility with pre-Java 5 bytecode. When you define a generic class or method, the compiler validates the types you use, but it strips these generic type parameters during the translation to bytecode. Essentially, the compiler replaces all type parameters with their bounds (or Object if unbounded) and inserts explicit type casts where necessary. This means that at runtime, the JVM has no knowledge of the specific type arguments used to instantiate a generic class; a List<String> and a List<Integer> are both represented as a raw List in the heap. This design choice was deliberate to allow legacy code to interoperate with generic code without breaking the JVM specification or requiring a massive re-engineering of the class file format.

items: The compiler replaces unbounded type parameters (e.g., <T>) with java.lang.Object, while bounded parameters (e.g., <T extends Number>) are replaced by the upper bound (Number).

Bridge methods are automatically generated by the compiler to maintain polymorphism when a class implements a generic interface or overrides a method with a specialized type, ensuring that the method signatures remain compatible at the bytecode level.

Because of erasure, you cannot perform 'instanceof' checks against parameterized types (e.g., 'list instanceof List<String>' is illegal) or create new instances of a generic type parameter (e.g., 'new T()').
Reflection on generic types is limited; while you can inspect generic signatures via the Reflection API, you cannot retrieve the actual type arguments of an object instance at runtime.

parsed_answer.content: A common 'gotcha' for senior engineers is the Heap Pollution warning. If you mix raw types with generic types, you can bypass compile-time checks, leading to a ClassCastException at a point in the code far removed from where the actual type violation occurred. Always avoid raw types in production code, and if you must interact with legacy APIs, use @SafeVarargs or suppress warnings only after rigorous validation of the collection's contents.
